It is a decent game with great ideas, but sometimes the execution could be better. At some points of the game i have totally no idea what needs to be done and yet there is a short timer ticking down, forcing me to replay a part of the game several times... Eventually ending up checking the walkthrough (and thinking "how am i supposed to know that")

The part i dislike the most is how you cannot skip cutscenes.

The game really can't decide if it wants to be puzzly or hold your hand constantly, even artificially blocking your progression until it deems you "ready".

The UX is outright abyssmal, with every action having some sort of artificial delay, like waiting for some voice line to finish, or have an arbitrary fake progress bar go up. This will happen dozens and dozens of times. It can not be turned off. It can not be skipped.

It adds up to a LOT of time wasted, even if you aren't forced to repeat them because of the random minute "quizzes" the game occasionally throws at you, marking the only time where the game won't let you look up anything. You remember exactly WHERE the info would be, but no - you have to game over, retry, look it up, go through 1 or 2 minutes of unskippable very mediocre voiced lines again, and only THEN are you allowed to progress... to the next question. Rinse and repeat, unless you literally memorized every single little remark and detail from dozens of random conversations and social media posts.

The game ist just so incredibly tedious to play. It actively doesn't want you to have any fun. The story could be decent enough I guess, but it's certainly not enough of a payoff for the awful, awful gameplay.
Missing a single piece of evidence in the end game is infuriating. The rest of the game is great, but the "you have to click EVERYTHING thing the dev thought was obvious" means I can't recommend it.

Fully recommend if you want to stimulate your brain!

This game has a couple of problems:
1. Some of the things you have to deduce are really far fetched. Like:
[spoiler]You're supposed to figure out which limb a person has injured by assuming that all people are right handed[/spoiler]. I needed to look that up, after like 20 minutes.
2. To get the achievement for each chapter you have to get all the evidence and the only way to get evidence is to hover over every text, because if it is evidence it will be marked red. This can be turned of in the settings, but that just makes it even harder!
3. While doing a dialogue you may need to know things along the lines of 'when does this person do x?' and you can't look it up while doing the dialogue which mean it's basically 'choose something random; it's the wrong choice; look it up; advance dialogue; repeat'. I'm sorry but it can't remember every minute detail that may or may not be relevant in a dialogue tree, 30 minutes down the line.
4. QoL features I wish the game had. These are not really a problem but would be nice:
  - The back, forward and reload buttons in the browser don't work.
  - You can't enter URLs in the browser
  - Sometimes the browser opens new tabs, sometimes it doesn't. Would be nice if 'new tab' was bound to middle mouse button and 'open here' to left click.
  - The password cracker, which seems to be made to be like a dictionary attack thingie, doesn't crack the password unless it has ALL information even if the information isn't contained in the password e.g. 
  "Name: Susi"
  "Date of birth: 1.1.1970"
  resulting password is '111970"
  It wouldn't need the name for that.
  - Sometimes text messages appear on both sides of account and sometimes they're only on one side e.g.
  You lock into Alice's and Bob's account and on Alice's account the conversation is
  A: "Hi long time no see"
  B: "Are you ghosting me?"
  
  And on Bob's account it's
  A: "Hi long time no see"
  B: "Are you ghosting me?"
  one day later
  B: "Sorry. Didn't see your messages. Here's the super secret info you need."
  A: "Thank you"
  - Calling a person before you're supposed to just tells you that they're not available currently.
  - Hacking things is less like a puzzle and more of 'type this into a text box, then you have 5 minutes to find what you want and if you don't succeed you restart and have to type the text into the box again'. Like it's actually type a text into a box. It's 'this is the password `ERGT467´ type this into the text box below'. The time limit just seems pointless and the having to repeat everything after you run out of time seems frustrating.

A great, story-focused hacking/detective game. Some of the translation can be off and it did affect me solving some of the more obtuse puzzles, but with a guide on the side, I found playing through the main campaign and two DLC campaigns to be a fantastic way to spend 20 hours or so.

Yes, just like other reviewers have said, if you like Orwell you will like this and really should pick it up.  Be warned though, if you're pessimistic about the direction of human society, this WILL reinforce those opinions, and many of the characters are so grotesquely evil and self-interested that it makes you question what justice for such people really looks like, and no matter what happens to them you know you cannot ever undo the damage these people have inflicted.

Unlike Orwell, each mission is a self-contained story, but some of the characters pop up in multiple missions and have ongoing character development throughout the game.

Also, it is a fair bit more difficult than Orwell.  There is an option to turn-off auto-highlighting of clues (the things that Orwell calls "data chunks") in the text so that you have to find them yourself, and you have to be VERY observant and notice things in the text and images that the game does not require you to specifically capture and does not specifically point out to you, but will crop up at a future point.  For example, you might have to phone a character to obtain extra information to progress the story, and you will have to use ALL the information you've read/seen in pictures about them  about them to get them to spill the beans.  There are various timed puzzles too, that are difficult to the point of erring on the side of unfair, but the game does allow you to re-attempt failed hacks so it's not a game-over, restart the mission at these points, which I appreciated!

Finally, yes, as others have mentioned, the English translation is not always good, but it wasn't so bad that it spoiled the game for me, and it is always clear to me what the story is trying to tell me.  More of a problem is some of the voice acting, which is a mixed bag.  Some of the actors are convincing, many are not.  I absolutely hated the voice actor for Austin Hill, in the mission "The Evidence Vanishes," and to be honest, it broke the immersion for me.  It would have been better to simply just show the text of that audio log rather than have it play out.

Overall though, for a small indie studio, Aluba have a done an amazing job with this game and I am giving it my full recommendation.

I am very much looking forward to the sequel, which should be out soon.  I didn't get a chance to play the time-limited demo unfortunately, but I do hope Aluba have improved on some of the elements that didn't quite gel in this first installment.

I want to like this, but there are a number of things that make it hard to recommend this:

* A majority of the game involves finding text that will highlight in red when you click it to allow you to "gather clues" -- which leads to clicking every line of text, just in case. At some points, you'll be missing a single clue and have to go slogging back through all that you've previously read to find the one little sentence or phrase that you didn't click to highlight and collect. 
* The translation to English is absolutely terrible. In some places, that actually makes trying to figure out what the game wants you to do more difficult.  
* There's also some comically bad voice acting at times. To make matters worse YOU CAN'T FUCKING SKIP the spoken dialogue scenes. This is particularly egregious because in many sections you have to listen to entire conversations before you can collect any of the evidence (that is, click every sentence trying to find what will be highlighted in red as clues). 
* At some points, you're asked to piece together what happens, but you CAN'T TAB BACK TO WHERE THE INFO YOU COLLECTED IS STORED TO FIND THOSE ANSWERS!
* While it can be satisfying to poke around to get the info you need in the investigation stages, some of the other minigames/puzzles are just not fun to play. This is particularly bad when you reach the final stage(s) of the game. I was on my way to 100% completion, but that final stage is a such a slog of *TIMED* minigames, I stopped playing the main story and moved on to the DLC (they were cheap, so I thought I'd give them a try).
* A few stages are timed, and although some portions are generous with how much time you're given, it definitely makes it far less fun.
* The main story takes a twist that is just... asinine. [spoiler] You discover you're not a real person, but an AI--just like the antagonist. [/spoiler] Seriously, it killed the immersion the gameplay and story had managed to build.

It's a very low cost game, and I did get some fun out of it--but I don't think I can, in good conscience, recommend it to others.

The stories are deep and the characters have a life to them, things seeming natural for them... with few exceptions.

reviews.review:
Cyber Manhunt, made by Aluba Studios, throws you into a world that is seriously challenging. This game is for the gamers who love a tough test. Story is not just about the corporate intrigue; it's a sinister journey into the digital abyss, human wickedness and immorality.

The puzzles are hard, really making you think and act fast, and even if you're used to playing games, this one might keep you on the edge of your seat. It's a tough journey that demands your attention and skill. 

The music fits the cool vibe, but the sounds will keep you on your toes. They add to the pressure, making the game as intense as the tests you'll face.

I wish there had been more investment in proper translations and voice acting. However, I find the content engaging enough to overlook these shortcomings.

If you're into collecting achievements like I am, start with the free DLC called "A Company Man of Titan" before jumping into the main story of Cyber Manhunt. This DLC is like a practice round – it helps you get the hang of the puzzles and strategies without giving away any spoilers. By getting a handle on the puzzles in the DLC first, you can save yourself from having to replay parts of the game over and over.

To sum it up, Cyber Manhunt is not just a game; it's a hard adventure for those who love a challenge. Aluba Studios made something awesome and tough. If you're ready for it, get ready for a wild ride into the digital world.

Cyber Manhunt falls disappointingly short of what I was expecting. While it's evident that the developers poured time and effort into this game, the end result is a mediocre experience. Nothing is horribly bad, but nothing is great either.

One of the major letdowns is the story line, which is... cliched. I could figure out where it was going almost beat-for-beat. The characters feel two-dimensional, and most of the time I could skip past their dialogue and just find the highlighted bits I was meant to find without losing anything meaningful from the parts I skipped. 
Sleuthing, he game's core mechanic, turns out to be a painfully limited and repetitive experience. The investigative elements promised are reduced to basic point-and-click tasks, and copy-and-pasting things into boxes. The puzzles lack complexity and fail to challenge the player's intellect, resulting a cycle that gets old after chapter 2.
The dialogue delivery is often wooden, making it difficult to immerse oneself in the story.

I can tell the devs really tried, which redeems this to a point, but the overall experience falls flat. With a more engaging story line and more diverse detective mechanics, Cyber Manhunt could have been a standout title.

I had fun in the game although it felt a bit repeating in the last 2 chapters. It doesn't need 24 hrs to finish. I didn't turn off the game when i went to sleep that's why I had a 24 hrs game time.
Stories and characters are set in a fictional western country. But characters act like Asians. Used some real life stories from China and Korea in the stories. Some characters' motivations are not very convincing.

Yeah this is pretty fun if you like this kind of game. A solid 7/10 If you have played similar (Orwell) then you'll enjoy this one too, even if the experience is a little more barebones.

I enjoyed it and had a great time, but it's one of these games the really annoys me. It lacks any form of polish and it really holds it back.

Honestly, a whole lot of decisions were clearly made in development that have resulted in what I can only describe as a lazy implementation, such as having to wait a long time to from clicking on data, to having it appear in your own 'journal'. They fixed this in the DLC but didn't patch it into the main campaign experience? Why? Someone decided it wasn't worth the dev time and the game is worse off for it.

I appreciate English is not the first language of the dev team, but there are multiple cases where writing doesn't make sense, subtitles are way off or text is malformed due to there not being space. There are also typos throughout the experience. How hard is it to hire a native English speaker to proof read the script? Again it just strikes me as lazy. And I won't even get started on the voice acting. Let's just say it leaves something to be desired...

There are lots of other little issues throughout the experience that just make you feel that the amount of care put into this project isn't high enough.

Some of the mini games throughout are unnecessarily hard and detract from the experience and story which is actually pretty good. 

Recurring characters, interesting twists and somewhat believable characters actually made me invested in each case, especially seeing how they are all intertwined. 

DLC is also good, with 'Home Sweet Home' actually being better than the campaign itself. Brilliant! And most of the issues I had with the main campaign were improved upon.

As I say I enjoyed this game, it just sucks to see a potential 9/10 end up being a solid 7. It's good enough that I'll likely buy their next game.

Enjoyable game.

~9 hours to complete (without DLC).
Some puzzles are a little obscure (wave-length matching? one very specific phone password), but the rest is very intuitive and compelling. The stories definitely hooked me and left me wanting for more every time I'd delve a clue further.
The game does lack a little bit of polish, the interface, while intuitive, does tend to be a little non-responsive at times. The translation to English is a little lacking in polish as well -- The intent and details are still very easy to understand, but the syntax and tone often feel off.

For someone that liked Ace Attorney and Hacknet, this feels like a nice fusion in the middle of both genres. Would recommend to a fan of both of these types of games, while staying wary of the lack of polish.

The cybersecurity elements of this game are somewhat realistic and simplified enough to be enjoyable, and should teach people well not to leave too many digital footprints in real life.

However, I find certain aspects of the game to be too difficult and poorly designed, such as:
1. certain game mechanics [spoiler]that came up out of nowhere with no prior training, and they are time-sensitive.[/spoiler]
2. Deduction/Reasoning phases where choices are sometimes ambiguous.
3. The inability to lookup certain information while scam calls/texts are in progress. 
4. in-game "search engine" that doesn't accept partially correct words. (For example: you have to type in "Aluba Studio" instead of just "Aluba" to get the correct results.)

reviews.review:
What could be an interesting game heavily bogged down by tedium.  At one point I couldn't progress for 30 minutes because I hadn't collected a random picture of a bed off a website.  The bed wasn't used for anything, and was only a promotional shot, but for whatever reason, it was critical to collect.  I also found the quizzes you take to solve a portion of the case to often not make sense as to the story I had gathered thus far.

I'm 2.5 hours in at this point and honestly have no interest in going back.

If you think about it, much of this game is just clicking on links and copy/pasting info. But it ends up being so much more. It is framed as a hacking sim, but really its more of a detective sim with some puzzles on the side. The story may not be to everyone's tastes, but I like the dark and mature commentary on big data in the future. It does it however through focusing on the people, which makes it connect to us... as people. It gets a little edgy, but I never felt it was unjustified. I had some gripes about how the text selection can be a bit finicky, but overall I really liked the story and the gameplay felt like a good complement to it.

reviews.review:
[h1] 8/10 [/h1]

Although Cyber Manhunt may appear to be a hacking simulation game, I believe it is more appropriate to call it a social engineering simulation game. Overall, the strengths and weaknesses of Cyber Manhunt are quite evident: it has an outstanding and thought-provoking storyline that is both contemporary and ironic, with significant real-world implications. However, its gameplay design may not satisfy all players.

If you do not know social engineering, this game can give you a glimpse into the popular social science of gathering information about others through various means. By unraveling the secrets and events behind each character through information gathered from various social media platforms, websites, emails, phone calls, and more, players can engage in activities such as hacking, deception, and disguises to gather intelligence. For players who enjoy puzzle-solving and have patience, Cyber Manhunt can provide an excellent gaming experience. Additionally, the game's storyline is quite deep, depicting various cybercrimes, school bullying, exchange of interests, and blackmail. The game connects the characters through numerous fragmented yet interconnected clues, presenting players with a captivating narrative filled with criticism, irony, reflection, and depth. It is definitely worth a try for any narrative game enthusiast.

The shortcomings of the game primarily lie in its gameplay design. The game itself is relatively short, and the process of collecting clues through mouse clicks takes up a significant portion of the gameplay time. Many puzzle mini-games added to enrich the game's content may not be particularly interesting. Although they diversify the gameplay, some players may find them off-putting. Players familiar with social engineering may also feel that the game's gameplay design and certain plot developments are somewhat contrived. Furthermore, the game's depiction of hacking techniques is rushed and lacks rigor.

Overall, Cyber Manhunt surprised me beyond expectations. I recommend it to those interested in social engineering but with limited knowledge, fans of realism, and enthusiasts of text-based adventure games. If you can accept its shortcomings, you will find that Cyber Manhunt offers great value. On the contrary, if you are not interested in its gameplay and storyline, there is no need to give it a try. It is worth noting that this game draws heavily on Osmotic Studios' Orwell series released in 2016, with the main difference being that this game focuses more on narrative description and characterization, while Orwell offers a stronger interactive gaming experience.

reviews.review: This game definitely has some outmoded ideas about women, sexual violence, abuse, etc. IT's a bit clunky to play as well and not all that realistic as far as hacking but it's entertaining

First mission into this game and we are already tasked with showing that a woman claiming to be a victim of domestic violence was actually a liar who commits marriage fraud and 'takes advantage' of men. We are forced to face a throng of 'social commentary' on how social media always takes the women's side and the innocent men have no chance to defend themselves and how he was actually loving and we should all pity him for committing suicide, despite the fact that we also learn that his company did tax evasion and created fake accounts to sway public opinion on a series of issues including the elections. Oh, yes, it's also telling that we discover that she was doing it because she was being forced to by her actual husband who she married to in college where she was an A student....but that was not collectible evidence because...who cares right?

I'm sorry, but I can't in right consciousness recommend that anyone finances this type of game with this insidious misogyny behind it.

Overall I enjoyed this game and was drawn to it because of the hacking theme. The story lines are interesting, and also on the mature side. The game play is fun, and I enjoyed the way the game prepared you to use the hacking tools and let you explore on your own. There were some parts of the game that I found a bit unbearable, like the long phone call audios and the parts where you called from anonymous number. Those sequences mainly called for using your best guess to choose the right voice prompt, and often I found it intuitive and just wanted to get it over with. Otherwise, I  enjoyed the hacking game play style of this game and the attention to detail in many small parts of the game.
